title: Frameworks handle server rendering for you

slides.text: You rarely call the server APIs yourself 🧰
slides.say: Render to pipeable stream, hydrate root, pre render. In a real app, you rarely wire these up by hand.

slides.text: For a new React app or website, the docs recommend starting with a framework, like Next.js (App Router) or React Router (v7).
slides.say: For a new app or website, the React docs recommend starting with a framework, like Next dot js with the App Router, or React Router version seven.

slides.text: A framework can call the react-dom/server APIs for you, and wires up hydration on the client.
slides.say: The framework can call the react dom server APIs for you, and it hydrates the page on the client too.

slides.text: Frameworks don't require a server. They support client rendering, single-page apps and static generation, and can be hosted on a CDN.
slides.say: And a framework doesn't force you to run a server. These frameworks support client side rendering, single page apps and static generation, deployed to a CDN or static hosting.

slides.text: Start client-only, then turn on server rendering per route when it makes sense, without a rewrite.
slides.say: So you can start with a client only app. Later, you can turn on server rendering for individual routes, without rewriting your app.
